### Cyrtomium laetevirens

#### (Hiyama) Nakaike

## (no common name)

## Dryopteridaceae

Cyrtomium laetevirens is a species of fern in the family Dryopteridaceae. It is native to South Korea and Japan, and is part of a species complex.

## Description

Cyrtomium laetevirens grows up to 100 cm tall and has erect or spreading rhizomes; rhizomes are densely covered with ovate-lanceolate, shiny dark brown scales with serrate margins. Leaves are odd-pinnate, papery in texture. The blade is 35 to 60 cm long and 14 to 20 cm wide, on a 25 to 35 cm long, dark brown stipe. The stipe is 2 to 3 mm in diameter, covered with lanceolate scales. The base of the leaf is slightly narrowed and the tip is gradually pointed. Fronds usually have 18 to 25 pairs of alternate, lanceolate leaflets. Side leaflets are 6 to 10 cm long and 1.8 to 3 cm wide, shortly stalked, narrowing continuously from the base to the tip. The base is slightly auriculate, with a “bump” on the side closer to the tip of the frond. Margins are minutely serrated. The upper surface of the leaf blade is shiny. Sori are borne on the undersides of leaflets; the indusia are untoothed, uniformly grayish white, about 1.2 mm wide (Lee et al. 2013).
Cyrtomium laetevirens is part of the Cyrtomium fortunei complex of species, which are closely related apogamous taxa (they produce spores without sexual fertilization) that have wide, often overlapping ranges of morphology and are difficult to identify (Ootsuki et al. 2011). This particular species is sometimes treated as a form of Cyrtomium fortunei that differs in having shiny leaf blades, but chemical evidence suggests that it may be a different species (Choi et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2013).
Other taxa in this complex include: C. fortunei, which has non-shiny leaf blades and many (15 to 30) pairs of pinnae; C. clivicola, which has non-shiny, light green leaf blades and 5 to 20 pairs of pinnae; C. atropunctatum, which has indusia that are dark brown in the center, and C. yamamotoi, which has indusia that are dark brown in the center and less than 15 pairs of pinnae (Ootsuki et al. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Posted by sbrobeson about 1 year ago  (2025-04-02T21:21:42Z)

As I understand it (based substantially on insights from @yuri_pirogov above):

  * The iNat taxon Iris × hybrida corresponds to Iris × hybrida hort., which encompasses bearded Irises of various parentage. There are about 2,000 iNat observations ID'ed as this taxon.
  * The plants identified as Iris × hybrida definitely do not correspond to Iris × germanica, either as used on iNat, or as defined by POWO with the hybrid formula I. pallida × I. variegata. Those are not the parents for the Iris × hybrida plants on iNat.
  * So, regardless of how we address Iris × hybrida, it would be entirely wrong to merge it into Iris × germanica. The proposed taxon swap should be cancelled.
  * Botanical nomenclature requires published nothotaxa to have a precisely identified combination of parents to be valid. The long history of horticultural Iris breeding and the multiple crosses involved mean that identifying exact parentage is very challenging. In order to group plants usefully, Iris specialists have made use of horticultural hybrid names that encompass all hybrids from a particular set of parents.
  * While future research and taxon descriptions may identify additional wild species and clarify hybrid parentage, it seems unlikely that we will ever get to a point where botanical nothospecies can be described for most of the plants contained within Iris × hybrida.
